name: Microsoft

header.one_liner: Azure is growing almost 50% and the order book is $677B; the price is the depreciation bill on the capex behind it.
header.thesis: Microsoft grew revenue 19% and non-GAAP EPS 18% in the September quarter, with Azure up 48% and commercial remaining performance obligations up 73% to $677B. Capex of $39.4B in the quarter nearly doubled. The question is whether returns on that spend hold margins as depreciation rises.

base.eps_label: FY2027E non-GAAP EPS (year to June 2027), excluding OpenAI gains and losses: Q1 actual $4.89 plus continued high-teens growth
base.rev_label: FY2027E revenue ($B): Q1 actual $92.3B plus sequential growth led by Azure

rev_cagr.why: Revenue grew 19% in the September quarter: Agents and Infra +25% with Azure +48%, Devices and Consumer -3%. Commercial remaining performance obligations of $677B (+73%) cover several years of cloud revenue. The base case fades growth from about 19% toward the mid-teens as Azure's base gets larger.
rev_cagr.source: Microsoft FQ1 2027 release; segment revenue from the 10-Q

margin_end.why: Non-GAAP net margin was 39.5% in the quarter. Capex of $39.4B in one quarter turns into depreciation over the next five to six years, so the base case lets margin slip about two points despite revenue growth. The bear case is AI pricing that does not cover the infrastructure cost.
margin_end.source: FQ1 2027 release (net income, capex); engine judgment on depreciation

share_chg.why: Buybacks of $4.4B in the quarter against a market value near $3.8T are about 0.5% a year, mostly offsetting employee share grants.

exit_pe.why: Today's multiple is about 25x fiscal 2027E EPS. The base case holds it, because growth accelerated this year; the bear case is a de-rating if AI capex stops earning its keep.
exit_pe.source: Engine judgment; current multiple computed from price and FY27E EPS

pillars.title: Azure is the growth engine
pillars.claim: Azure grew 48% and Microsoft Cloud 30% to $63.9B, the fastest growth in several years.
pillars.test: Does Azure growth stay above 35% as the base grows?

pillars.title: The order book is enormous
pillars.claim: Commercial remaining performance obligations rose 73% to $677B, several years of cloud revenue under contract.
pillars.test: How much of the backlog sits with a single AI customer?

pillars.title: Capex is doubling
pillars.claim: Additions to property and equipment were $39.4B in the quarter; free cash flow fell to $18.6B on $58.0B of operating cash flow.

evidence.t: Cash from operations $58.0B; additions to property and equipment $39.4B

pillars.test: Does operating margin hold near 50% as depreciation rises?

pillars.title: The consumer side is shrinking
pillars.claim: Devices and Consumer revenue fell 3%, with Windows OEM and devices down 22%.

evidence.t: Devices and Consumer $15.5B, -3%; search and advertising ex TAC +12%

pillars.test: Is the PC decline cyclical or structural?

variant.street: The market pays about 25x fiscal 2027 earnings for accelerating cloud growth and a $677B order book.
variant.ours: Growth is excellent and well covered by contracts. The engine's base case holds the multiple and lets margin slip on depreciation, and still compounds EPS in the mid-teens: on an unchanged multiple that beats the cost of equity.
variant.could_be_wrong: If AI services earn software-like margins, depreciation is absorbed easily and earnings grow faster than revenue.
variant.would_change_mind: Azure growth below 35% while capex keeps rising, or operating margin below 45%.

moat.summary: Enterprise distribution, the Microsoft 365 installed base and one of three hyperscale clouds.
moat.detail: Rated from the latest 10-K and 10-Q; see the moat window for the sources of advantage.

quality.leverage_note: Net cash: cash and investments about $64.5B against debt of about $35.5B at 30 September 2026.
checks: Non-GAAP excludes only OpenAI investment gains and losses: Q1 GAAP EPS $4.92 vs non-GAAP $4.89
Free cash flow $18.6B in the quarter, down as capex doubled

tripwires.text: Azure growth below 35% in a quarter

risks: One customer is a large share of growth.

lenses.eisman: Ask how much of the $677B backlog is one AI lab, and what happens to the capex if that customer slows.
lenses.munger: A great business spending like a utility. The test is whether returns on capital stay high.

lenses.hohn: Monopoly-like positions in productivity software fund the cloud build; check the incremental return on capex.

review.basis: Fiscal Q1 2027 10-Q (quarter to 30 September 2026) and release. Q2 reports in late January; this review refreshes after the print.
review.headline: The best-positioned AI platform, growing faster than a year ago. The return clears the cost of equity, but our numbers are close to the Street’s; the risk is the depreciation bill.
review.model: Microsoft sells cloud computing (Azure), workplace software (Microsoft 365, Teams, Dynamics, LinkedIn) and consumer products (Windows, Xbox, Bing). Most revenue is recurring subscriptions sold to businesses.

how_it_earns.v: Rents computing, storage and AI capacity. Billed on use. The growth engine.
Per-user subscriptions for Office, Teams, security and Copilot.
Bing and Edge advertising, net of payments to partners.
PC licences, Surface and gaming. Cyclical and shrinking.

mix.note: Revenue by product line as tagged in the 10-Q. Fiscal 2027 introduced two reporting segments: Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer.

review.position: One of three hyperscale clouds with Amazon and Google, and the leader in enterprise productivity software.

moat.threat: AI could shift where value sits in software; the capex race could lower returns for all three clouds.

what_numbers_say.d: $39.4B of additions to property and equipment in one quarter; free cash flow $18.6B.
Devices and Consumer -3%; Windows OEM and devices -22%.

balance.read: Net cash, AAA-rated. The balance sheet is not the constraint; free cash flow is.
facts: Cash and investments about $64.5B vs debt about $35.5B
$10.2B returned in the quarter: $6.8B dividends, $4.4B buybacks
Large finance and operating lease commitments for data centers

flags.evidence: Non-GAAP removes the equity-method impact of the OpenAI investment: +$0.03 to GAAP EPS this quarter, -$0.41 a year earlier.

flags.flag: Free cash flow falling while earnings rise
flags.evidence: Operating cash flow $58.0B less capex $39.4B gave $18.6B of free cash flow in the quarter.
The 73% rise in commercial RPO likely includes large multi-year AI contracts; the customer split is not disclosed.

forecast_basis.margin_end: Judgment: depreciation from the capex step-up takes about two points

base.story: Azure growth slows gradually from 48%; depreciation takes a little margin; EPS grows mid-teens.

downside.story: AI demand slows while depreciation keeps rising; margins fall and the multiple compresses toward 20x.
downside.needs: Azure below 30% with capex still rising

upside.story: AI services earn software margins; operating leverage returns and the multiple expands.

risks.how: Capex nearly doubled to $39.4B a quarter. If AI prices fall faster than costs, depreciation erodes margins.

risks.cause: One customer is a large share of growth
risks.how: Much of the backlog growth likely comes from multi-year AI contracts. A slowdown at one large customer would cut Azure growth.
Azure growth is limited by how fast data centers and power can be added, not only by demand.
Windows OEM and devices fell 22%; a longer PC slump drags on the consumer segment.
Competition authorities in the US and Europe are examining cloud licensing and AI partnerships.

peer_read.why_premium: Microsoft has the highest EBITDA margin among the clouds, net cash and the largest enterprise software base.
peer_read.why_not: Alphabet grows faster on consensus with Google Cloud doubling, and trades at a lower multiple.
peer_read.peers_note: Oracle's multiple is low because heavy capex and debt make its earnings less certain.

Is 25x fair for earnings growth in the high teens?

arguments.label: Growth
arguments.text: Revenue grew 19% in the September quarter, Microsoft Cloud 30% and Azure 48%. Commercial remaining performance obligations rose 73% to $677B.

thesis_long: Microsoft is the best-positioned large company for enterprise AI. It owns the software most businesses already pay for, one of three hyperscale clouds, and a large stake in the leading AI lab. Growth accelerated this year: revenue +19%, Azure +48%, and a $677B order book that covers years of cloud revenue.

The cost is capital. Additions to property and equipment nearly doubled to $39.4B in the quarter, and free cash flow fell to $18.6B even as net income rose. That spend becomes depreciation over the next several years, so margins depend on AI pricing staying above the cost of the infrastructure. Some of the backlog likely sits with a small number of very large AI customers.

Our base case lets growth fade toward the mid-teens and margin slip about two points, with the multiple held near 25x. EPS still compounds in the mid-teens, which beats the cost of equity over 12 months. But our estimates sit close to consensus, so that return reflects our cost of equity rather than something the market is missing, and without a variant view we hold the call at Equal weight. We would turn positive if operating margin held near 50% while capex rose, and negative if Azure growth fell below 35% with capex still climbing.

upside_risks.how: If Copilot and AI agents are priced like software, revenue would grow faster than depreciation and margins would rise.
A visible peak in capex would lift free cash flow quickly and support a higher multiple.

dcf.label: Operating EPS. Free cash flow is held down by the AI capex build, so on free cash flow the growth the price implies would be higher still
